---
title: "Competing risks"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  out.width = "100%",
  dpi = 96
)
```

Often a patient can have one of several events, and having one rules out the
others. In `pbc3`, a patient with primary biliary cirrhosis can die or receive
a liver transplant; once transplanted, the patient can no longer die of the
untreated disease. These are *competing risks*. Treating the competing event
as censoring overstates the risk of the event of interest, so BJM models both
event types together and predicts the risk of each.

This article covers every step of an analysis with two competing event types:

| Step | Function | With competing risks |
|---|---|---|
| Look at the data | `cifPlot()` | cumulative incidence of each event type |
| Fit | `survivalSub()` | adds a model for the event type |
| Fit | `longitudinalSub()` | unchanged; the biomarkers may depend on the event type |
| Predict | `predictRisk()` | the risk of each event type |
| Predict | `predictLongitudinal()` | the biomarker's future value, given no event of either type |
| Predict | `predictPlot()`, `riskPlot()` | both risks in one plot |
| Simulate | `simulateTrajectory()` | the event time *and* type of each simulated future |
| Evaluate | `performancePlot()`, `calibrationPlot()` | AUC, Brier score and calibration per event type |

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(BJM)
data(pbc3)
```

## The data

`pbc3` has one row per visit. Three columns describe the outcome, and they are
constant within a patient:

* `years`: time from registration to the event or to censoring;
* `status3`: 1 if the patient had *an* event (death or transplant), 0 if
  censored;
* `status4`: the event type, 0 for death and 1 for transplantation, and `NA`
  for a censored patient.

(`status5` codes the same information in one column, 0 censored, 1 death and
2 transplant, which is the form `cifPlot()` takes.)

```{r data}
first <- pbc3[!duplicated(pbc3$id), ]
table(event = first$status3, type = first$status4, useNA = "ifany")
```

Of the 312 patients, 140 died, 29 were transplanted and 143 were censored. The
cumulative incidence of each event type, estimated with the Aalen--Johansen
estimator, treats the other event correctly rather than as censoring:

```{r cif, fig.alt = "Cumulative incidence curves with 95% confidence bands for death and transplantation over 15 years of follow-up; death reaches about 0.6 while transplantation levels off near 0.1."}
cifPlot(pbc3, survival_variable = "years", event_type_variable = "status5",
        event_labels = c("1" = "Death", "2" = "Transplant"))
```

## Step 1: the survival sub-model

The backward joint model writes the joint distribution of the event time $T$
and the event type $D$ as

$$
P(T, D) = f(T) \, P(D \mid T),
$$

a model for when *some* event happens, and a model for which event it is
given when it happens. `survivalSub()` fits both, from one row per patient:

* `form_marginal_surv`, a Cox model for the time to the first event of either
  type (`status3`);
* `form_conditional_cr`, a logistic regression for the event type (`status4`)
  among the patients who had an event. It must contain the event time
  (`years`), as a plain linear term: this is how the chance of each type can
  change over time.

```{r survival-sub}
survival_fit <- survivalSub(
  first,
  form_marginal_surv = Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex,
  form_conditional_cr = status4 ~ years + age + sex
)
survival_fit
```

"Cause 1" is the event type coded 0, death, and "cause 2" the type coded 1,
transplantation, the same order the predictions below use. The event-type
model's coefficients are log odds of transplantation against death: older
patients are much less likely to be transplanted, while the timing of the
event makes little difference (`years`, p = 0.75).

```{r plot-survival, fig.alt = "Forest plot in two panels: hazard ratios of the survival model, where age is slightly above 1 and sex is below 1 with a wide interval, and odds ratios of the event-type model for age, sex and event time, all close to 1 except age, slightly below 1."}
plot(survival_fit)
```

Without competing risks, leave `form_conditional_cr` out (or set it to
`NULL`): every prediction below then refers to the single event.

## Step 2: the longitudinal sub-models

The biomarker models do not change. As usual, they are fit on the patients
with an event, whose event time is known, and contain the event time
(`years`) as a covariate:

```{r longitudinal-sub}
long_sub_fixed <- list(
  "serBilir" = serBilir ~ year + age + sex + years + years:year,
  "albumin"  = albumin  ~ year + age + sex + years + years:year
)
long_sub_random <- list("serBilir" = ~ year | id, "albumin" = ~ year | id)
long_fit <- longitudinalSub(pbc3[pbc3$status3 == 1, ], long_sub_fixed, long_sub_random)
```

A biomarker may also depend on the event type, if its course before a death
differs from its course before a transplant. Add the event-type column to the
formula:

```{r longitudinal-by-type}
long_fit_by_type <- longitudinalSub(
  pbc3[pbc3$status3 == 1, ],
  list(serBilir ~ year + age + sex + years + years:year + status4,
       albumin  ~ year + age + sex + years + years:year + status4),
  long_sub_random
)
```

The event type is unknown for a patient being predicted; the predictions
average over it, so the prediction data does not even need a `status4`
column.

## Step 3: the risk of each event type with `predictRisk()`

As in `vignette("BJM-intro")`, we predict for patient 2 from their visits up
to year 5. The outcome columns are unknown at that time, so they are set to
`NA`.

```{r patient}
patient <- pbc3[pbc3$id == 2 & pbc3$year <= 5, ]
patient$years <- NA
patient$status4 <- NA
```

`predictRisk()` returns one risk per event type: the probability that the
patient's *first* event happens within `horizon` years of `prediction_time`
and is of that type, given that they were event-free at `prediction_time`
and given their biomarker history.

```{r predict-risk}
risk <- predictRisk(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
                    prediction_time = 5, horizon = 3, time_variable = "year",
                    survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
risk
```

* `risk_prob_1` is the risk of event type 0 of `status4`, here **death**;
* `risk_prob_2` is the risk of event type 1, here **transplantation**;
* their sum is the risk of an event of either type.

Which event is `_1` and which is `_2` follows the coding of the event-type
variable: `_1` is its value 0 (or its first level, for a factor). Recode it
if you want the event of interest first.

The sum is the risk of an event of either type, which is also what a model
without the event-type part predicts. Here the two agree exactly, because the
biomarker models do not depend on the event type, so summing over the types
just gives back the single-event model:

```{r compare-total}
survival_fit_any <- survivalSub(first, Surv(years, status3) ~ age + sex, NULL)
risk_any <- predictRisk(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit_any,
                        prediction_time = 5, horizon = 3, time_variable = "year",
                        survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
c(death = unname(risk$risk_prob_1), transplant = unname(risk$risk_prob_2),
  sum = unname(risk$risk_prob_1 + risk$risk_prob_2), any_event = unname(risk_any$risk_prob_1))
```

Several patients can be predicted at once; patients who already had an event
before `prediction_time` are left out.

```{r predict-several}
several <- pbc3[pbc3$id %in% c(2, 4, 5, 9) & pbc3$year <= 3, ]
several$years <- NA
several$status4 <- NA
risk_several <- predictRisk(list(several, several), long_fit, survival_fit,
                            prediction_time = 3, horizon = 3, time_variable = "year",
                            survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
round(data.frame(death = risk_several$risk_prob_1, transplant = risk_several$risk_prob_2), 3)
```

The model with type-specific biomarker courses is used the same way. Its
risks differ a little, because the history now also says something about
which event is coming:

```{r predict-risk-by-type}
risk_by_type <- predictRisk(list(patient, patient), long_fit_by_type, survival_fit,
                            prediction_time = 5, horizon = 3, time_variable = "year",
                            survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
c(death = unname(risk_by_type$risk_prob_1), transplant = unname(risk_by_type$risk_prob_2))
```

## Step 4: future biomarker values with `predictLongitudinal()`

`predictLongitudinal()` predicts a biomarker's value at `prediction_time +
horizon`, for a patient who is still event-free then. With competing risks
this means free of *both* events; the prediction averages over the event
types (and times) the patient may have later, weighted by how likely each
is.

```{r predict-longitudinal}
bilirubin <- predictLongitudinal(bio_i = 1, list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
                                 prediction_time = 5, horizon = 1, time_variable = "year",
                                 survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
bilirubin
```

`bio_i` picks the biomarker (`1` is `serBilir`); with several, or `NULL`, all
of them are predicted in one call.

```{r plot-longitudinal, fig.height = 3.5, fig.alt = "Predicted density of patient 2's log bilirubin one year after year 5, a single bell-shaped curve with a dashed line at its most likely value, near 1.2."}
plot(bilirubin)
```

## Step 5: plotting a patient's risks

`predictPlot()` fixes the landmark and lets the window grow: it shows the
biomarker history, the predicted future biomarker, and the risk of each event
type as the horizon increases (event type 1 is death, event type 2
transplantation).

```{r predict-plot, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Prediction plot for patient 2 at year 5: the observed bilirubin history up to year 5, the predicted future bilirubin with widening uncertainty bands from year 5 to 8, and the predicted risk of the two event types growing with the horizon, death to about 0.25 by year 8 and transplantation staying near 0."}
predictPlot(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
            prediction_time = 5, horizon = seq(0, 3, 0.5), time_variable = "year",
            survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
```

`riskPlot()` instead fixes the window, here one year, and moves the landmark,
so each risk uses more of the history:

```{r risk-plot, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5.5, fig.alt = "Patient 2's bilirubin history from year 0 to 5 together with the predicted one-year risks of the two event types at landmarks 1 to 5; the risk of death rises slowly as bilirubin increases, and the transplantation risk stays near 0."}
riskPlot(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
         prediction_time = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), bio_i = 1, horizon = 1, time_variable = "year",
         survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list())
```

## Step 6: simulated futures with `simulateTrajectory()`

`simulateTrajectory()` draws complete futures from the model. With competing
risks each draw has an event time *and* an event type, in the `status4`
column:

```{r simulate}
sims <- simulateTrajectory(list(patient, patient), long_fit, survival_fit,
                           prediction_time = 5, times = seq(5, 12, 0.5), time_variable = "year",
                           survival_variable_all = list(), survival_trans_function = list(),
                           n_sim = 500, seed = 1)
draws <- sims[!duplicated(sims$sim), ]
table(type = draws$status4, event = draws$event, useNA = "ifany")
```

The cumulative incidence of each event type computed from the draws is a
patient-specific version of the `cifPlot()` above:

```{r simulate-plot, fig.alt = "Cumulative incidence of death and transplantation for patient 2 after year 5, computed from 500 simulated event times: death rises to about 0.83 by year 14.3, mostly between years 8 and 11, and transplantation stays below 0.05."}
plot(sims, which = "event")
```

## Step 7: evaluating the predictions

`performancePlot()` and `calibrationPlot()` report the time-dependent AUC,
the Brier score and the calibration of each event type separately; see the
[Plotting with BJM](plotting.html) article for an example on held-out data.

## Things to watch for

* **Two event types.** The event-type model is a logistic regression, so BJM
  handles two competing event types. Combine rarer types, or model them one
  against the rest.
* **The coding of the event type** decides which risk is `risk_prob_1`
  (value 0, or the first factor level) and which is `risk_prob_2`.
* **Censored patients** have an `NA` event type. They are used by the Cox
  model but not by the event-type model, and not by the biomarker models,
  which are fit on the patients with an event.
* **The event time in the event-type model** must be a plain linear term
  (`years`, not `log(years)` or a spline): the predictions integrate over it.
* **The outcome columns are unknown for a new patient.** Set `years` and
  `status4` to `NA` in the prediction data, or leave `status4` out.
